mcqs.q: Why is infiltration less reliable in the mandible than in the maxilla?
opts: Lower-tooth roots are embedded in thick, dense compact bone
The mandible has no nerve supply
Mandibular bone is more porous than the maxilla
The IAN runs outside the bone
mcqs.explain: The dense compact bone of the mandible resists diffusion, so nerve blocks (e.g. IANB) are usually preferred over infiltration.

mcqs.q: The lingual gingiva and floor of the mouth are supplied by the:
mcqs.explain: The lingual nerve supplies the lingual gingiva and floor of the mouth; the IAN supplies the teeth/bone and the long buccal the molar buccal gingiva.

mcqs.q: The IAN and lingual nerves can be anaesthetised together by a single injection at the:
opts: Medial side of the ramus (pterygomandibular space)
mcqs.explain: Both nerves lie at the medial side of the ramus; the IAN sits in the pterygomandibular space just before the mandibular foramen.

mcqs.q: An inferior alveolar nerve block (IANB) anaesthetises the mandibular teeth from the:
opts: Central incisor to the third molar on that side
mcqs.explain: An IANB numbs all mandibular teeth (incisor to third molar) on the injected side, plus the lip, chin and (via the lingual nerve) tongue/floor of mouth.

mcqs.q: The IANB is notable for having the:
opts: Highest positive-aspiration rate (10–15%) of intraoral injections
Lowest failure rate of all blocks
mcqs.explain: The IANB has the highest positive-aspiration rate (10–15%) and a relatively high failure rate (15–20%).

mcqs.q: An IANB is contraindicated in a very young or mentally handicapped patient mainly because they may:
opts: Bite the anaesthetised lip or tongue
mcqs.explain: The wide soft-tissue anaesthesia risks self-inflicted lip/tongue injury in patients who cannot avoid biting.

mcqs.q: The deepest depression on the anterior border of the ramus, used as an IANB landmark, is the:
mcqs.explain: The coronoid notch is the greatest depression on the anterior ramus; an imaginary line runs from it to the pterygomandibular raphe.

mcqs.q: During an IANB, the syringe is directed from the opposite-side premolars and bone is contacted at a depth of about:
opts: 20–25 mm, then 1.5 mL is deposited after negative aspiration
mcqs.explain: Bone is contacted at 20–25 mm; withdraw ~1 mm, aspirate, and slowly deposit 1.5 mL for the IAN (then 0.2 mL on withdrawal for the lingual nerve).

mcqs.q: If an IANB fails because the solution was deposited below the mandibular foramen, you should:
mcqs.explain: Depositing below the foramen is a common failure; correct it by reinjecting 5–10 mm above the previous site.

mcqs.q: Incomplete pulpal anaesthesia of the mandibular first molar after an IANB is often due to accessory supply from the:
mcqs.explain: The mylohyoid nerve (not normally blocked by the IANB) is a common accessory supply, leaving the mesial of the first molar partly sensate.

mcqs.q: A bifid inferior alveolar nerve is a recognised cause of:
mcqs.explain: A bifid IAN (two canals) can leave part of the supply un-blocked, causing partial anaesthesia.

mcqs.q: Trismus (limited mouth opening) after an IANB is usually caused by:
mcqs.explain: Post-injection trismus is commonly due to medial pterygoid muscle injury/soreness.

mcqs.q: Transient facial paralysis after an IANB (drooping lip, inability to close the eyelid) results from depositing LA into the:
opts: Parotid gland, blocking the facial nerve (CN VII)
mcqs.explain: LA deposited into the parotid gland blocks CN VII (motor to facial muscles), causing temporary unilateral facial paralysis.

mcqs.q: Why does an IANB require a separate long buccal injection for molar extractions?
opts: The long buccal nerve is not anaesthetised by the IANB
The IANB only numbs the tongue
The buccal nerve is part of the lingual nerve
mcqs.explain: The long buccal nerve (anterior division of V3) supplies the molar buccal gingiva and is not blocked by an IANB, so a separate injection is needed.

mcqs.q: The long buccal nerve block is given where the nerve crosses the:
opts: External oblique ridge, distobuccal to the last molar (depth 1–2 mm, 0.3 mL)
mcqs.explain: Inject where the buccal nerve crosses the external oblique ridge, distobuccal to the last molar at the occlusal level — only 1–2 mm deep, 0.3 mL.

mcqs.q: The Gow-Gates technique is described as a 'true mandibular nerve block' because it:
opts: Anaesthetises the entire V3 distribution (IAN, lingual, buccal, mylohyoid, etc.)
Numbs both sides of the mandible
mcqs.explain: Gow-Gates (≈90% success) blocks the whole mandibular division — IAN, lingual, mental, incisive, mylohyoid, auriculotemporal and buccal (in 75%).

mcqs.q: In the Gow-Gates technique, the needle is advanced until it contacts the:
mcqs.explain: The needle (aligned corner-of-mouth to intertragic notch) is advanced ~25 mm to the condylar neck; LA is deposited only after bone contact.

mcqs.q: The Akinosi technique is specifically useful for patients who:
opts: Have limited mouth opening (e.g. trismus, infection, trauma)
mcqs.explain: The Akinosi (closed-mouth) V3 block is performed with the mouth closed, ideal for patients with limited opening from trismus, infection or trauma.

mcqs.q: In the Akinosi block, the needle bevel is oriented:
opts: Away from the ramus (so it deflects toward the ramus, near the IAN)
mcqs.explain: Orienting the bevel away from the ramus makes the advancing needle deflect toward the ramus, keeping it near the IAN in the pterygomandibular space.

mcqs.q: After a mental nerve block, gentle massage over the foramen is done to:
opts: Push solution into the foramen to also block the incisive nerve
mcqs.explain: Massaging the area drives the solution into the mental foramen, blocking the incisive nerve and numbing the premolars/incisors as well as the lip/chin.

mcqs.q: The mental foramen, target of the mental block, lies below the apices of the:
mcqs.explain: The mental nerve exits the mental foramen below the apices of the lower premolars; the needle is inserted 5–6 mm to bone and ~0.6 mL deposited.

mcqs.q: For a mandibular labial infiltration, the solution deposited at bone is about:
mcqs.explain: Insert at the crossing of the mucobuccal-fold and long-axis lines at 45°, advance to bone, aspirate and slowly inject 0.6–0.8 mL without ballooning the tissue.

mcqs.q: During lingual infiltration, the needle should be kept near bone to avoid:
opts: Injuring the blood vessels in the floor of the mouth
mcqs.explain: Keeping the needle close to bone (depositing 0.3–0.5 mL just below the mucosa) avoids injuring the vessels in the floor of the mouth.

mcqs.q: Tingling/numbness of the lower lip after an IANB primarily indicates anaesthesia of the:
mcqs.explain: Lip tingling/numbness reflects mental (IAN terminal) nerve anaesthesia; tongue tingling reflects lingual nerve anaesthesia.

mcqs.q: If an IANB fails because the needle was placed too far anterior on the ramus, the correction is to:
opts: Redirect the needle tip more posteriorly
mcqs.explain: Too-anterior deposition is corrected by redirecting the needle tip posteriorly toward the foramen.

saqs.q: List the areas anaesthetised by an inferior alveolar nerve block.
saqs.a: Mandibular teeth (incisor→3rd molar) on that side, mandibular body/inferior ramus, chin and lower lip, premolar/incisor labial gingiva, and (via the lingual nerve) the anterior ⅔ of the tongue, floor of mouth and lingual gingiva.

saqs.q: Give the IANB landmarks and key depths.
saqs.a: Landmarks: coronoid notch, pterygomandibular raphe, occlusal plane. Insert ¾ of the way from finger to raphe; contact bone at 20–25 mm, deposit 1.5 mL (IAN) + 0.2 mL on withdrawal (lingual).
Deposition below the foramen (reinject higher), needle too far anterior (redirect posteriorly), accessory mylohyoid supply, and a bifid inferior alveolar nerve.

saqs.q: List the complications of an IANB.
saqs.a: Haematoma (medial ramus; pressure + cold), trismus (medial pterygoid injury), and transient facial paralysis (LA into the parotid blocks CN VII).

saqs.q: Describe the long buccal nerve block.
saqs.a: A separate injection (the IANB doesn't block it) where the buccal nerve crosses the external oblique ridge, distobuccal to the last molar at the occlusal level — depth 1–2 mm, 0.3 mL; for buccal soft tissue of the molars.

saqs.q: Contrast the Gow-Gates and Akinosi techniques.
saqs.a: Gow-Gates — open-mouth true V3 block (~90%), needle to the condylar neck (aligned corner-of-mouth → intertragic notch). Akinosi — closed-mouth V3 block for limited opening; needle 25 mm into the pterygomandibular space, bevel away from the ramus.

The mental nerve exits the mental foramen below the premolar apices; insert 5–6 mm, deposit ~0.6 mL at bone, then massage to drive solution into the foramen (also blocks the incisive nerve) — numbing premolars/incisors, labial bone, lip and chin.
